utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. I would like to check first of all if the interpreters are all ready? Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can they hear me? Can everybody in the court hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do my colleagues hear me, the Prosecutor and the Defence? Does the accused hear me in a language which he understands? Does he hear me now in a language he understands?

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can I ask the Registrar to call out the number and the name of the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-96-22, the Prosecutor versus Drazen Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. We can now commence with this hearing. Further to the decision of the Appeals Chamber on 7th October 1997 and the order of the President on 20th November 1997, the case of Drazen Erdemovic has been remitted to this Trial Chamber. Today we will be taking the reply of the accused to the charges made by the Prosecutor against him in the indictment dated 22nd May 1996. Could the accused please rise and state for the Trial Chamber his name, date and place of birth, and the name of his attorney?

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Drazen Erdemovic, I was born on 25th November in Tuzla, and my lawyers are Mr. Babic and Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you confirm to the court, Mr. Erdemovic, that you have had time to confer with your lawyer on the various issues concerning this case and that you are satisfied with the legal advice that you have been receiving so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am satisfied with the legal advice I have been receiving from my lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Can we have appearances for the Prosecution, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Mr. McCloskey and Ms. Sutherland for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I have appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Jovan Babic, attorney, member of the bar of Vojvodina, which is within the Serbian bar of attorneys, and an advisor in the bar of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours, my name is Nikola Kostic, I am an attorney from the United States licensed to practise in that country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. For these proceedings, the accused is charged with one count of a crime against humanity and an alternative count of a violation of laws and customs of war. Can I ask the Registrar to read the indictment against Mr. Drazen Erdemovic, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, pursuant to his authority under Article 18 of the Statute of the Tribunal, charges Drazen Erdemovic with a crime against humanity or alternatively a violation of the laws and customs of war, as set forth below: 1. On 16th April 1993, the Security Council of the United Nations, acting pursuant to Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter, adopted Resolution 819, in which it demanded that all parties to the conflict in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina treat Srebrenica and its surroundings as a safe area which would be free from any armed attack or any other hostile act. Resolution 819 was reaffirmed by Resolution 824 on 6th May 1993 and by Resolution 836 on 4th June 1993. 2. On or about 6th July 1995, the Bosnian Serb army commenced an attack on the UN 'safe area' of Srebrenica. This attack continued through until 11th July 1995, when the first units of the Bosnian Serb army entered Srebrenica. 3. Thousands of Bosnian Muslim civilians who remained in Srebrenica during this attack fled to the UN compound in Potocari and sought refuge in and around the compound. 4. Between 11th and 13th July 1995, Bosnian Serb military personnel summarily executed an unknown number of Bosnian Muslims in Potocari and in Srebrenica. 5. Between 12th and 13th July 1995, Bosnian Muslim men, women and children who had sought refuge in and around the UN compound in Potocari were placed on buses and trucks under the control of Bosnian Serb military personnel and police and transported out of the Srebrenica enclave. Before boarding these buses and trucks, Bosnian Muslim men were separated from Bosnian Muslim women and children and were transported to various collection centres around Srebrenica. 6. A second group of approximately 15,000 Bosnian Muslim men, with some women and children, fled Srebrenica on 11th July 1995 through the woods in a large column in the direction of Tuzla. A large number of the Bosnian Muslim men who fled in this column were captured by or surrendered to Bosnian Serb army or police personnel. 7. Thousands of Bosnian Muslim men who had been either separated from women and children in Potocari or who had been captured by or surrendered to Bosnian Serb military or police personnel were sent to various collection sites outside of Srebrenica including, but not limited to, a hangar in Bratunac, a soccer field in Nova Kasaba, a warehouse in Kravica, the primary school and gymnasium of 'Velko Lukic-Kurjak' in Grbavci, Zvornik municipality and diverse fields and meadows along the Bratunac-Milici road. 8. Between 13th July 1995 and approximately 22nd July 1995, thousands of Bosnian Muslim men were summarily executed by members of the Bosnian Serb army and Bosnian Serb police at diverse locations including, but not limited to, a warehouse at Kravica, a meadow and a dam near Lazete and diverse other locations. 9. On or about 16th July 1995, Drazen Erdemovic and other members of the 10th sabotage detachment of the Bosnian Serb army were ordered to a collective farm near Pilica. This farm is located north west of Zvornik in the Zvornik municipality. 10. On or about 16th July 1995, Drazen Erdemovic and other members of his unit were informed that busloads of Bosnian Muslim civilian men from Srebrenica, who had surrendered to Bosnian Serb military or police personnel, would be arriving throughout the day at this collective farm. 11. On or about 16th July 1995, buses containing Bosnian Muslim men arrived at the collective farm in Pilica. Each bus was full of Bosnian Muslim men; ranging from approximately 17-60 years of age. After each bus arrived at the farm, the Bosnian Muslim men were removed in groups of about ten, escorted by members of the 10th sabotage detachment to a field adjacent to farm buildings and lined up in a row with their backs facing Drazen Erdemovic and members of his unit. 12. On or about 16th July 1995, Drazen Erdemovic did shoot and kill and did participate with other members of his unit and soldiers from another brigade in the shooting and killing of unarmed Bosnian Muslim men at the Pilica collective farm. These summary executions resulted in the deaths of hundreds of Bosnian Muslim male civilians. The accused. 13. Drazen Erdemovic was born on 25th November 1971 in the municipality of Tuzla. He was a soldier in the 10th sabotage detachment of the Bosnian Serb army. He is currently in custody in the UN detention facility in The Hague. General allegations. 14. At all relevant times to this indictment, a state of armed conflict and partial occupation existed in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. 15. Drazen Erdemovic is individually responsible for the crime alleged against him in this indictment pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Individual criminal responsibility including committing, planning, instigating, ordering or otherwise aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation or execution of any crimes referred to in Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal. Charges. Counts 1-2 (crime against humanity) (violation of the laws or customs of war). 16. By his acts in relation to the events described in paragraph 12, Drazen Erdemovic committed: Count 1: A crime against humanity punishable under Article 5(a) (murder) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Alternatively Count 2: A violation of the laws or customs of war punishable under Article 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal and recognised by Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions. Signed Richard J Goldstone, Prosecutor, 22nd May 1996, in The Hague, the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As there are two alternative charges to which the accused has to plead, my colleagues and I have decided that an explanation of the differences of the charges is required. Briefly, a war crime is a violation of the laws and customs of war. A crime against humanity can also be constituted by similar conduct as a war crime. But it is an attack of a widespread or systematic nature on the civilian population. The Appeals Chamber in dealing with the appeal by the accused determined that a crime against humanity is more serious than a war crime and therefore carries a heavier penalty. Will you please rise, Mr. Erdemovic? In the charges against you, there are alternative charges, and you have options as follows. You may plead not guilty to both charges; or as these charges are in the alternative, you may plead guilty to either one or the other, and not guilty to the other charge. Do you understand the content of the indictment and the charges against you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Have you discussed these charges with your lawyer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Has he explained them to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is there anything about which you are not clear concerning these charges against you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: There is nothing that is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would still emphasise that it is very important for you to understand the legal position and the choices available to you and the consequences of whatever decision you may take in making your pleas, but before proceeding further, can you please sit down, Mr. Erdemovic? Can you just sit down? Before proceeding further, I would like to discuss the question of motions. The Trial Chamber has seen the motion raised by Defence counsel in his letter of 3rd December and is aware of other developments. Mr. Babic, can you confirm your position? Are you maintaining your motion as raised in your letter and would you like us to consider it now or later?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I suggest that both my motions, the one of 3rd December and the one that I submitted yesterday, regarding the goals and elements of the sentence and the annex of the motions -- to the motion which I also submitted yesterday, that they should both be discussed today and if I can speak to -- if I can argue those, I would do that, provided you do not have other preliminary questions; in other words, my suggestion is that we discuss the motions now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What you mean is that we discuss these motions before the plea is taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I would also like to make a statement. During the drafting of the motions and my preparation for the complete defence of my client, that is the accused Erdemovic, and my efforts to contribute to the Trial Chamber's gaining the full picture of the full scope of the guilt and responsibility of Erdemovic, I studied the issue of reformatio in peius, and I also submitted yesterday as part of the annex to the motion a study of the Supreme Court of Yugoslavia, as well as other High Courts in the Republics of the former Yugoslavia, which support the thesis that I have set out, and I have also filed a motion on aims and elements for the determination of sentence. Based on my work on these two motions and the annex, together with my learned colleague Kostic, I co-operated with the Prosecution, especially as relating to the Article 11 of the US federal law, and I have determined that it would be reasonable and that it would be very important that I withdraw both my motions today, and have it replaced by the agreement which we have drafted together with the Prosecution, and this is my initial statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much: the Trial Chamber confirms that you have withdrawn both motions and you are relying on the joint motion with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Prosecution, any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. We note what has been said by counsel and we affirm there is an agreement which has been entered into between the parties which we have filed for your Honours' consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just like to add one thing. I would like to explain why this was done by the Defence. It was done because the Defence was not clear which procedure and which system we were going to follow before this Trial Chamber, and when we concluded that so far the common law practice was the guiding system, this is when we decided on this which we have just presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Trial Chamber does take note of the plea agreement as confirmed by both parties, and as the parties themselves acknowledge, we are not bound by the terms of this agreement, but we will, of course, take it into very careful consideration, the issues raised by both parties. We do however wish to have confirmation from the accused as to whether he understood the agreement, that he entered into it voluntarily. Mr. Erdemovic, will you please stand? I am sure you have understood what your counsel has just stated to the Trial Chamber, that he has withdrawn his two motions and that he confirms the agreement entered into with the Prosecution just now. I would like to ask you whether you are aware of this agreement yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am aware of the agreement and I have signed it and I am aware of everything that is written down in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am going to put to you the charges against you. As I have already explained, there is count 1 and then in the alternative count 2. Count 1, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(A), murder, of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you plead? In pleading I wish to have the words, "I plead not guilty", or "I plead guilty". So to count 1, crime against humanity, how do you plead?

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: On count 1, I plead not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The alternative count, which is count 2, a violation of the laws or customs of war, punishable under Article 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal and recognised by Article 3(1)(a), murder, of the Geneva Conventions, how do you plead?

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I plead guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Erdemovic. Before the plea of guilty is recorded, I would like to find out from you whether you had sufficient time to discuss your plea with your counsel, with your lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do you agree that the manner in which you have pleaded to the alternative count which is count 2 is in accordance with the instructions of your lawyer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I would also like to be sure whether any pressure was put on you, either by the Prosecution or indeed your own counsel to plead guilty to count 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other outside sources, any pressure from anybody else besides the Prosecution and the Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do you realise the consequences of pleading guilty under our Statute? We take into account the sentencing practices of the courts of the former Yugoslavia and our own Statute. In that regard, we can impose a sentence of life imprisonment on you. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, Mr. Erdemovic. I would now like to hear the Prosecutor's reaction to the plea of guilty to count 2, and also hear submissions on the requirements imposed by Rule 62 bis (C). Is there a sufficient factual basis for the crime and the accused's participation in it and if so, what are the facts, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, as was contained in the agreement that we submitted for your Honours' consideration, the Prosecution accepts that a plea of guilty to the charge of a war crime is in accordance with the agreement that was entered into between the parties. Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that there is ample evidence in support of the plea and in support of the charges, and in that regard, we have filed with your Honours some material which was previously tendered in this matter, which facts do not in any way differ from what we would put forward at this stage, so if your Honours please, there is a motion that we filed on 8th January 1998, and contained within that there is the transcript of the sentencing hearing that took place before Trial Chamber I on 19th to 20th November 1996, and we submit that for your Honours' consideration as facts that may be taken into account in a consideration of this plea. In addition to that, your Honours, there is transcript of the guilty plea itself before the Chamber on 31st May 1996, which we have also filed before the Chamber and we respectfully submit that for your Honours' consideration, having regard to the facts of this matter. There is also submitted for your Honours' consideration two psychological evaluations, one of 24th June 1996 and one of 14th October 1996, and we respectfully submit that all of this material, taken into consideration, form an adequate basis for the allegations in the Prosecutor's indictment and form the facts on the plea that we would submit to you for consideration in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Niemann, but because this is a replea, these are fresh proceedings, the Trial Chamber would still appreciate a brief statement of the facts which support the indictment to which the accused has pleaded guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There are the facts that are set out in the indictment, in particular paragraphs 2 through to 12 of the indictment, which we rely upon. Would your Honour excuse me a moment? (Pause). There is also the facts contained or referred to in paragraph 11 of the agreement that was entered into by the parties. To briefly go over the factual basis of this matter, your Honours, I take your Honours to the initial decision of the Chamber which heard this matter, and where it decided upon certain of the facts of the case. It was found there, your Honour, and these facts we rely upon and there is no dispute by the Prosecution and I understand by the Defence as to them, that on 16th July 1995, when the accused, as a member of the 10th sabotage detachment of the army of Republika Srpska, participated in the shooting of approximately 1200 unarmed Muslim civilians at the Branjevo farm near the village of Pilica. The Pilica farm is near a building in Zvornik. These are the facts which, in addition to those that we have referred to, we rely upon in this plea. As I have said earlier, it has been agreed between the parties that those will represent the facts for the purposes of this agreement, so unless there is any other matters that I can assist your Honours with, I do not think that I can take you to anything other than -- other than read material out to you which has already been submitted, but I am happy to do that if your Honours would like me to read out the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that is sufficient. The references to the materials and the paragraphs in question are sufficient. The Defence, do you agree to what the Prosecution has stated before the court, the facts in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are prepared and do stipulate and agree to the facts that were outlined by Mr. Niemann. We also know the contents of the documents that he referred to, as does our client, so we would agree to all of those submissions, including Mr. Niemann's oral presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: The first Trial Chamber, when passing its judgement, in the text of its decision, there was a vague reference which actually brought about suspicion that the 10th sabotage unit of the Bosnian Serb army was also involved in the execution of 500 Muslims in the social hall in Pilica. This part of the judgement was brought into question by the Defence during the appeal, because the 10th sabotage detachment did not take part in these killings. We would just like to hear from the Prosecutor whether they still insist that Drazen Erdemovic had anything to do with this act of the 10th sabotage detachment, which was not involved in the massacre in Pilica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Prosecution, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. My name is Peter McCloskey. Mr. Babic is correct, there was some confusion in the record regarding the two incidents of massacres that occurred on this day. The one that Mr. Erdemovic was involved in occurred at Pilica farm during the entire day, and then after that was through, a detachment of people from another brigade went into the town of Pilica and participated in the murdering of 500 individuals. It is our understanding and belief that the facts do not show that Mr. Erdemovic was involved in that in any way. I believe the confusion was not in the factual record from the testimony but perhaps how it was interpreted. There was some confusion, he is correct, but to make it clear today, those are the facts, Mr. Erdemovic was not involved in that second massacre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Erdemovic, please stand. You have heard what the Prosecution has said as to what the facts are to the charges on the plea -- on the charge to which you have pleaded guilty. You have also heard what your counsel Mr. Babic has said and the correction he has put in as regards the facts found by the previous Trial Chamber. I would like you to answer the Trial Chamber, whether you agree with the facts as stated by the Prosecution and agreed to by your counsel, subject to the correction, on the count in which you have pleaded guilty, do you agree to the facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I completely agree with the Prosecution and with my counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. (Pause). Very well then. There are no questions from my colleagues. The Trial Chamber has determined that the plea of Drazen Erdemovic is valid. Drazen Erdemovic, this Trial Chamber now formally accepts your plea of guilty and directs the Registrar to record that fact. The Trial Chamber convicts you on count 2 of the indictment, a violation of the laws or customs of war, punishable under Article 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal and recognised by Article 3(1)(a), murder, of the Geneva Conventions. Can the Prosecutor please confirm that he is withdrawing the other charge?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we confirm we withdraw the crime against humanity count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Registrar, please enter the conviction and note the withdrawal of count 1. At this stage, it is necessary to make arrangements for pre-sentencing hearing to enable the parties to submit any relevant information that may assist the Trial Chamber in determining an appropriate sentence. I understand from the Registrar that the courtroom is available, should we wish to hear any submissions of the parties later this afternoon or even tomorrow. Are the parties in a position to proceed to make their submissions on sentencing this afternoon, after a short recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The Prosecution is ready, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: As far as the Defence is concerned, the Defence is also ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The court will adjourn for a short period, 30 minutes, before we go into sentencing hearings. Thank you. The court will rise. (3.20 pm) (A short break) (3.50 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The proceedings have resumed. I would like to check if the interpreters are ready.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do my colleagues hear me? The Prosecutor and the Defence? Thank you. Does the accused hear me in a language he understands?

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can I ask the Registrar to call out the number and the name of this case again, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-96-22-T bis, the Prosecutor versus Drazen Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are now commencing the pre-sentencing hearing. We have already recorded a plea of guilty as stated by the accused. In accordance with the decision of the Appeals Chamber and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the conviction has been recorded. We are now proceeding to Rule 100 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence to enable the parties to submit any relevant information which may assist the Trial Chamber in determining the appropriate sentence to be imposed on Mr. Erdemovic. I would like to call upon the parties to indicate which way they would like to go, whether they intend to lead evidence for this proceeding, or whether they have any documents which they would like to rely upon. May I ask the Prosecution first?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. We have a transcript of the evidence that Mr. Erdemovic gave at the hearing pursuant to Rule 61 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which we would seek to tender or make available to the Chamber in relation to what we have to say about mitigation. We will suggest that the extensive nature of the evidence he gave is a mitigating factor, so I hand that to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I would like to hear from the Defence counsel, please. You have heard what the Prosecution have said and the document they have put in. Do you agree, or do you have anything else to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing I would like to add is we anticipated that this document would become a part of the record and we will stipulate and agree to it and its admission for your use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In addition your Honours, also dealing with the issue of mitigation, we have available today to call Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez, who is an investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor, and he could attest to the significant co-operation that has been provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by Mr. Erdemovic, and that may be a matter that would assist your Honours in addressing the sentence in this matter. Should your Honours feel that that would assist, we have him here available and we can call him. My colleague Mr. McCloskey would ask him some questions. In addition to that, I can address your Honours shortly on the matter of sentencing, if that would be of assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would propose doing that before calling -- before we call the witness, if that is an acceptable course to your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Niemann. You can go ahead with your proposal. You can address the Trial Chamber and then call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish to address you only shortly on these matters but to assist you to refer to Article 24(2) and Article 7(4) of the Statute of the Tribunal, and Rule 101 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, all of which in our submission go to the question of imposing a sentence. If your Honours please, the relevant factors mentioned in those provisions deal with such issues as the gravity of the offence, the individual circumstances of the convicted person, whether the accused was following superior orders, any aggravating circumstances, any mitigating circumstances, and substantial co-operation with the Prosecutor by the convicted person. Your Honours, I do not think it is necessary for me to deal with aggravating circumstances, I think the facts speak for themselves, and I do not think it is necessary for me to go further than just to direct your Honours to those facts for that purpose. Likewise, with respect to the gravity of this offence, it should not be necessary for me to labour that, your Honours, as it is so obvious from the facts of the matter. However, because it is such a serious crime, and because the circumstances are so aggravating and so serious, it is I think necessary for us to, as the Prosecutor, to place some emphasis on the question of mitigation, because that is a factor which needs to be balanced against the heavy aggravating circumstances that your Honours need to consider. Your Honours, Mr. Erdemovic has been of considerable assistance to the Office of the Prosecutor. Firstly, in respect of surrendering himself to the Tribunal in The Hague. It is true that he was transferred to the Tribunal upon request, but it should be noted that he was already in the process of coming to The Hague before he was arrested by officials in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which ultimately resulted in him being transferred here. I think what is significant is that he had already made the initial steps to surrender and come to The Hague, and in respect of that, your Honours, we would submit that that is a significant matter, having regard to the historical difficulties that have confronted this Tribunal in having persons arrested and brought before the Chamber. Your Honours, shortly after Mr. Erdemovic came to the Hague, he voluntarily confessed to his crimes to an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor. During the course of speaking to members of the Office of the Prosecutor, he expressed his genuine remorse for his actions which occurred on July 16th 1995. This combination of factors, his efforts to surrender himself, his confession of guilt, and his expression of remorse, which has been accepted as genuine, your Honours, are in our submission mitigating factors. Your Honours, in addition to those mitigating factors, your Honours may wish also to consider that he acted pursuant to superior orders when he carried out this crime, a crime in that the order he was given was criminal in its nature, but he was complying with superior orders. That is a factor your Honours may consider is appropriate mitigation when determining any sentence. Your Honours, the issue of substantial co-operation with the Office of the Prosecutor is a matter which in our submission does justify considerable mitigation. We say that because the position of the Office of the Prosecutor cannot be directly equated to that which occurs in national jurisdictions, in the sense that in national jurisdictions the prosecutor officials have access to police forces who are mobile on the ground and can obtain evidence and information much more readily and easily than occurs with the Office of the Prosecutor here in the Tribunal, which to a large extent is dependent upon the co-operation of states and other international and non-international bodies, before that information can be collected and gathered. Because of those constraints upon the Prosecutor in bringing before the Chamber the evidence of these cases, it is significant when an accused person provides assistance and co-operation, because without that assistance and co-operation, it is often the case that the Office of the Prosecutor would not otherwise be able to present these matters before the court. Indeed, your Honours, in relation to this particular -- the events in this particular case, the Office of the Prosecutor had no information directly in relation to these, in particular the details about the Branjevo farm in Pilica where these 1200 souls were murdered. That information was not available to the Office of the Prosecutor in any great detail prior to the assistance that was given by Mr. Erdemovic. The location of the site was significantly -- of significant importance to the Office of the Prosecutor and permitted an exhumation to be carried out at that site where the victims were uncovered. Not all of the victims were uncovered, but it would seem that a large number of them may have been removed. There is also the events that occurred in the cultural hall in Pilica. The accused himself was not involved in this incident at all, he was merely a witness to the events, but it was again a tragic circumstance where some 500 people, 500 civilians were murdered, and Mr. Erdemovic witnessed this and he gave evidence of this event to the Office of the Prosecutor. Again, this is an incident that the Office of the Prosecutor was not aware of prior to the assistance that was given by Mr. Erdemovic. In addition to that, your Honours, he has given us names and identities of other perpetrators to a number of crimes, the details of which I cannot go into for obvious reasons, but your Honours, that has led to active investigation by the Office of the Prosecutor which continues to this moment. I tendered, your Honours, the information, I should say the transcript of the evidence that Mr. Erdemovic gave in the course of the Rule 61 hearing into the indictments of Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. Mr. Erdemovic very courageously gave evidence in relation to these very significant persons who have been indicted by the Tribunal and he gave that evidence freely and voluntarily and at some personal risk in so doing, and in our submission, your Honours, that is another factor that we would suggest to you may appropriately be considered in mitigation of any sentence that may be imposed upon him. Your Honours, Rule 101(B)(iii) states that the Trial Chamber should take into account the general practice regarding prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia. We previously provided an analysis of this and addressed it previously, if your Honours please, and indeed probably, having regard to the agreement that has been reached between the parties in relation to the view that the Office of the Prosecutor takes on sentencing, which I emphasise is merely a matter for your Honours to consider or reject as you please, but it probably has little significance, but it is worth noting that in the former Yugoslavia, this type of crime would be punishable by a term of imprisonment between 5 and 20 years, so 5 being the minimum and 20 years being the maximum. Your Honours, the only matter that I would finally wish to address to you is the fact that having regard to the fact that Mr. Erdemovic now faces sentence in relation to a war crime, as opposed to the more serious crime of a crime against humanity, which is a more serious crime, the Office of the Prosecutor wishes to indicate for your Honours' consideration that so far as our view was concerned, an appropriate sentence would be seven years' imprisonment. As I say, I emphasise, that is a matter for your Honours to consider. Unless I can be of any further assistance, I would seek the assistance of my friend, Mr. McCloskey, to call the witness, Mr. Ruez, who has spoken to Mr. Erdemovic on numerous occasions and who has been provided with considerable assistance as an investigator of the Tribunal. If your Honours please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We shall proceed to hear the witness as stated by Mr. Niemann. Mr. McCloskey, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I would refer you to the lengthy testimony of investigator Jean-Rene Ruez at the sentencing hearing when he covered the length and breadth of this case, but for the purposes of this proceeding, we wish to concentrate on Mr. Ruez's testimony on the three most significant mitigating factors to give you some understanding what the factual basis is for those three factors that were just gone over by Mr. Niemann. Those are, just for your knowledge, they are in the plea agreement between the parties in paragraph 13, 14 and 16(c), and I will just briefly refer to those. There is the voluntary appearance by Mr. Erdemovic, before we even knew Mr. Erdemovic existed or Branjevo farm existed; then the value of his co-operation to the Prosecution and lastly that the Prosecution feels that he was acting under superior orders and under duress and that should be taken into account in mitigation. Mr. Ruez can give you some of the background facts and is open, of course, for your questions on that and anything else you wish to talk to him about. Without further ado, I would call Jean-Rene Ruez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Registrar will administer the oath. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You may take the oath. JEAN-RENE RUEZ (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel? Examined by MR. McCLOSKEY

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please state your name and spell it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Jean-Rene Ruez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may sit down. Could you tell the court your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a French judicial police superintendent working at the Office of the Prosecutor since April 1995 as an investigation team leader now for the Srebrenica investigation, which started in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you been the team leader for that investigation since the inception of that investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The court has just been prepared to hear your responses on three basic issues that go to mitigation regarding the conduct of Mr. Erdemovic. You also will be questioned perhaps on any other issues regarding the case, but the first issue that I want to ask you about, and we will just go directly to it, is: did the Prosecution know anything about Mr. Erdemovic prior to Mr. Erdemovic's surfacing in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, before his first contact with a French journalist, we did not know about him and most certainly if he had not come to The Hague, we would never have heard about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the judges the circumstances, how he happened to come forward and what you have learned about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What we know about it is mostly coming from Mr. Erdemovic himself, but also from the people he was in contact with when he made several attempts to get in touch with the Tribunal at that time. When he was in Belgrade, he used a colleague of his as an intermediary with several people in an effort to gain access to the Tribunal and come and explain the situation in which he has been put during the events at Branjevo farm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he finally able to get an audience with some press people through this intermediary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did. Unfortunately for him, these events led to his arrest by the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and so he has been arrested and later on, we have requested him to be transferred to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court how his contact with the press resulted in his arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had to make several attempts. At that time there was no office of ICTY in Belgrade, therefore he had to contact several of our organisations and press people. The multiplication of his attempts have raised attention on him and this is why at one point he got arrested before we could gain direct access to him in that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was he interviewed by the press?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was interviewed by the press, he gave a full story about the situation he wanted to report to the Tribunal. He slipped some things we went on to correct, he did that on purpose at that time because he wanted to be sure everyone would respect that part of the deal and once he had told the story to these people, their part of the contract would also be fulfilled and they would arrange transportation for him to go to The Hague and explain that directly to us. Later on we sorted out all these little differences between the statements he gave to the press and to us and on all these points he gave very clear and direct decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shortly after his contact with the press, were ICTY able to interview the press person that had interviewed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we took a statement from one of these press persons and we have it in the records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the information provided by the press person consistent with what Mr. Erdemovic has been saying all along in his other statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, the story is nearly equivalent to the one that he told us, there is no major difference, and he was also requested several times if he was aware of the fact that he might be held responsible for the actions he was communicating with us, and he told to these people that he knew that he may be held responsible, but he was accepting this responsibility and insisted on his will to come to The Hague and testify about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shortly after his arrest in the former Yugoslavia and the Prosecution became aware of his existence, did the Prosecution and Mr. Erdemovic -- excuse me. Did Mr. Erdemovic then agree to come to The Hague from the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did and as soon as he arrived here, he reproduced the story he had to tell and then we entered in a lot of details and he was never reluctant to enter into these details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was represented by Mr. Babic during that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, during the first main statement, if we can call it so, Mr. Babic was present, but we had also several contacts without the presence of his counsel, but with the agreement of Mr. Babic, who gave us a waiver so that we could communicate with Drazen Erdemovic for the needs of the investigation at any moment and this is what we did on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Unless the court has any particular questions about that first of three elements of mitigation, I would go on to the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I should find it more agreeable, counsel, if you would conclude your examination and then leave it to the judges to consider whether they wish to put any questions. I would not personally wish to segment the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Ruez, can you briefly describe to the court what kind of co-operation Mr. Erdemovic has provided the investigation and how valuable that has been to the investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The collaboration of Drazen Erdemovic has been absolutely excellent. He has repeated the things that he told previously to others before his arrival at the Tribunal, he has always entered in all the details we wanted him to enter. At the beginning it was extremely painful for him, because now he is in a much better physical and mental condition than he was at his arrival. At the beginning entering again all these details was extremely painful for him, but he did it and even went sometimes above the collaboration that we were expecting from him. As an example, when he was watching the television in his cell and he pinpointed some events or individuals he knew and knew about the crimes that they had committed in the context of the Srebrenica operation, he let us know about it and we could interview him on the subject and deepen the subject and he was always very willing to collaborate with us on these points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He also testified at the Rule 61 hearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure, he testified also during the Rule 61 hearing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that testimony consistent with what you had learned from him in previous statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. In addition also to this, to make clear the points on which he has assisted this investigation and some points which we would probably have not known about it without his assistance is of a massacre which was committed at the Pilica house of culture. It is a situation about which we had no other sources except his testimony, and this enabled us to find the location and to conduct a crime scene analysis of the location, and it was a totally new event for those who are conducting this investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Has Mr. Erdemovic also promised to continue his co-operation in the future, including testifying and providing any other information he knows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. His obvious motivation is not to please the Office of the Prosecutor to get some weakening of his possible punishment, he was very clear on that point since the beginning. He wants the truth to be known about these events and he wants the people who are responsible for these events to face justice one day, and there is no doubt that if that day happens, he will confirm the information that he has given to us until now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on his conduct thus far and his co-operation, do you have any reason to believe he will fail to live up to that proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On the third point, can you give the judges some of the background into the actual incident that leads you to believe that there was duress present when he committed these crimes and that this duress should be used as mitigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a personal belief that indeed he was under duress at that time, but the reason for that would need to re-explain a certain number of facts, which have probably for some of them not been raised in front of a court until now. He knew about the behaviour of some of the members of the unit he was part of, the unit was split into two locations, one was in Bijeljina and one was in Vlasenica. The rumour he was aware of was that members of the unit in Vlasenica had committed numerous crimes since the beginning of the war. It was public knowledge inside the unit. He also witnessed occasions where under the order of a commander, people were killed only because the order was given. He was himself in a very difficult situation at that time because of his ethnic background he was not fully trusted by his comrades. Also he already had some strong arguments with his commanders, because he did not fulfil the assignments he was given. The reason why he did not fulfil them was that for especially one of them, there was a big risk of civilian casualties and he did not fulfil the assignment, which led that he was stripped from his rank, so he was already at that moment in a very weak position in front of his superiors and also in front of his comrades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for one second. Could you describe just factually, briefly, how he found himself when he first came to the Zvornik area and with his squad and where they went and just the factual circumstances of this situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The factual circumstances of the situation, we know them also only through his testimony, was that on the morning of 16th July, he was designated to go with a few men to Zvornik, he did not know about the assignment at that moment. The fact is that the team leader of the group was a member of Vlasenica platoon which is not normally his own chain of command. The reason is that the man who was designated team leader had a close relationship with the commander of the unit and was part of these people who committed allegedly and according to the rumour bad actions since a couple of years. When he arrived in Zvornik, a lieutenant colonel came out of a building which is currently the Zvornik brigade headquarters. He was accompanied by two military policemen and led the team of the 10th diversion unit to the Branjevo farm where the civilians arrived and the assignment was given to execute all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you been to that farm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it as described by Drazen Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the location is as described by Drazen Erdemovic. Even before his arrival in The Hague, the first information which he gave to the press enabled us to collect additional intelligence and pinpoint the location of this farm and also gain access to some photographic evidence which was presented during the public hearing of July 1996, which confirmed already at that time the version of the facts as it was explained by Drazen Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I interrupted you as you were explaining other factors that you felt led to duress. I do not know if you can recall back where you were, but is there anything else you recall from the facts that you have learned that would lead you to believe he was really under duress when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is more or less also the whole context of the situation at that time. He participated in the military operation, of the takenover of the safe haven of Srebrenica, and also knew from his colleagues when he came back from a funeral in Trebinje, where he went for the funeral of one of his comrades who had been killed in an accident during that operation, he learned at that time that a lot of events had happened during his absence. He knew that when he was at the farm and all these buses were arriving, understood very quickly that all this was part of a quite huge operation and it would be out of the question for him to rage against it. Most certainly he would get in very deep trouble if he had done so, so he made a few attempts, but very quickly found out that it was absolutely unuseful and even received the command that if he was sorry for these people, he could line up with them. At that point, he made the choice to participate in this, not to be killed either on the spot, either very shortly afterwards and also had in mind the will to protect his wife and his kid, who were both in Bijeljina at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Unless you have anything further to add to this issue, I would have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. That is the end of the evidence from this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Defence counsel? Cross-examined by MR. KOSTIC

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Ruez, you have been a police officer for a long time, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For ten years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A part of your job and your training has to do with interrogating, interviewing and working with witnesses and accused, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This has happened on many occasions, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you began to work with Mr. Erdemovic, it was something that you had done before and you were quite familiar with it and quite good at it, I would imagine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if I was good at it, but I was quite familiar at it, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me as a general figure, how many times did you speak with Mr. Erdemovic and perhaps tell us the number of hours, just roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have my records with me so it is difficult to answer very precisely, but I would say that we had maybe ten contacts. Some of them were fairly long, nearly one day, others were one afternoon. Some were very formal because it was interviews, video interviews, interviews which were recorded, other situations were a presentation of videotapes, attempts of recognition of people, situations, and some even more informal circumstances where it was only aimed to clarify some points or some discrepancies between the way the story had been reported by the press people he was in contact with and the way he was explaining the situation to us. All these points have always been clarified in a very straight way and without any hesitation, which makes me believe that the man is indeed very credible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not only credible, but he has been very co-operative with you, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very co-operative with us, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both Mr. Erdemovic and Mr. Babic feel comfortable with the process so that you had access to Mr. Erdemovic whether Mr. Babic was present or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, for the reason of the investigation, we could have access to him at any moment. We were for sure always informing Mr. Babic that we would have these contacts, but there was never any problem with that. As I said, even on some occasions he came straightforward to us to provide us with information that we did not even pinpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your opinion that Mr. Erdemovic did not hold back any information when he was co-operating with you in regard to the events in Srebrenica and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, just to clarify one thing, you testified about the fact that Mr. Erdemovic had some contacts with journalists.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Subsequently, it is my understanding that one of them, a Vanesa Vasic Janekovic, wrote a letter to the Tribunal, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is right. She is the person who gave an interview also to the Tribunal about the context of this first meeting with Drazen Erdemovic, and also wrote this letter very recently about it. That was confirmed to us in March 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the gist or the highlight of that letter was the fact that before Mr. Erdemovic made his statements to the journalists, this person, Vanesa Vasic, told him on a couple of occasions that if he made the statements that he did, he could end up being responsible as a participant in these crimes, and somehow if arrested to be taken to The Hague to the International Criminal Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. More than that, she told him that he would be most probably held responsible and would face trial. It is indeed what happened, and he was very aware of this since the beginning and also in the course of our communication with him, he has never tried to bargain anything, he has never asked if his collaboration would be of help for him in judicial terms, all the judicial process has also had no influence on his behaviour. Whenever the moment we chose to have an interview of him or a contact with him, the fact that there was an appeal ongoing or any trial situation had never any interference, so his behaviour has always been the same and he always collaborated with us in the same spirit, whatever happened around the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That co-operation was important to you, was it not, because you could then use his statements to collaborate and really make sure that some of the events that he testified about actually happened. He gave you such detailed information, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He enabled us to corroborate other witness testimonies that we had. As we explained to the court during the first sentencing, there were some survivors from the massacre at the Branjevo farm, so we already had some information about it and this enabled us to check what Mr. Erdemovic was telling us, and the situations were described more or less in the same way, and also enabled us to find things that we would most probably not have found without him. Anyhow, at this stage of the investigation, we would not have found about it. I am thinking especially about the house of culture in Pilica, in which he did not participate but witnessed the event from a cafe where this same lieutenant colonel took them after the massacre at the Branjevo farm. He refused to participate in this next killing. He was followed in that by the members of the killing squad, but other individuals who were coming from Bratunac volunteered for that assignment and committed these killings. Mr. Erdemovic was witnessing this event from a distance of about 100 metres, and could give us a certain number of details about the location which enabled us to find the place and the crime scene was perfectly preserved even one year after the events happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is true that his statement then was corroborated by in fact scientific evidence that you gathered in regard to that house of culture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely the crime scene analysis, some of them are still on process, are confirming the story that he told us about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to ask you a little more difficult question, I think. As you spent all the time that you did with Mr. Erdemovic, you must have at some point discussed other things with him, such as his feelings about what he did, feelings about his family, feelings about the war, feelings about the position that he was in. Did you not get to that point with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not talk too much about feelings. His feelings were extremely obvious when he arrived here. He was in a very heavy state of stress and each time he was talking about details, he was again in a state of shock and we never entered too much about feelings, we stick more or less on facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Like a good policeman, right? But if I can just move it a bit along, he did express to you at times feelings of remorse, sorrow for what happened to the people at Srebrenica, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: More than once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More than once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those feelings of sorrow and remorse, do you feel they were genuine, real, that he really was going through that process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have personally no doubt on that. He is extremely angry against the people who have put him in that situation and his own motivation at this moment, I think it is still the same one, it is to designate these individuals and ensure that we will have enough material to bring them to trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is your belief that Mr. Erdemovic will continue to co-operate with you and with the Prosecutor's Office as these cases go on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether or not he signed an agreement which is in front of me does not matter, he will continue to co-operate with you and give you information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no doubt of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any clarification by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, your Honour, though I do believe we have a copy of the letter from the journalist, perhaps Defence counsel has it and we will make that an exhibit for your reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I have one copy, so I would be happy to tender it to the court, if there is no objection. Apparently there is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we would be pleased to receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: It is not in such good shape, your Honour, I apologise. We will tender it nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I hope it will be numbered appropriately. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, I have only one or two small questions to put to you. One concerns the arrest of Mr. Erdemovic in Serbia. He was, to your knowledge, a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnian Croat, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bosnian Croat. Yes, that is an important distinction and I must not forget it. Thank you. You have been engaged in investigative work for some number of years now, connected with the functioning of the Tribunal, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A member of the Office of the Prosecutor since April 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just enlighten me on one thing? Would I be right in supposing that the Serbian authorities arrested other persons in connection with allegations of the commission of war crimes of one kind or another in the Bosnia-Herzegovina area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of any arrest which is connected with the investigation I am in charge of and which has happened in Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, with the exception of Mr. Kremenovic, who was arrested at the same time as Mr. Erdemovic for sheltering a criminal and Mr. Kremenovic was in possession of weapons at that time and has been charged for that as well, but these are the only two individuals I am aware of, and we are aware of, which have been arrested in connection with the Srebrenica events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic complimented you, I am sure correctly, on the efficiency with which you have been performing your functions. Would I be in order in supposing that had the Serbian authorities made any other arrests of the kind to which I am alluding, that fact would in the normal course have come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard for me to answer this question. I am not part of the Belgrade authorities, so I do not know --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, but you are an investigative officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure I understand very well the question, but on that topic, there is something quite significant that you might be willing to learn. That is that we could have corroborated a little bit more the events as they have been explained by Mr. Erdemovic. Unfortunately, we have requested the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to hand over to the Tribunal the videotape which was stolen from the journalist who gave an interview to the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I think you are going into an area that is foreign to the purpose of my question, so I would suggest that we might shift to another matter. May I at this stage enquire from counsel on both sides about one matter? We have had put in evidence the record of the Rule 61 proceedings, mm? Have we had put in evidence the record of the previous proceedings on 19th and 20th November 1996 relating to this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I submitted those at the opening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You would regard them as forming part of the record of these proceedings, and the Defence counsel as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You would have given evidence on 19th November before Trial Chamber I.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your evidence, you would have referred then as you refer now, to the statement by the accused that he, in effect, acted under duress.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On 16th July 1995, there were, as I understand it, two main events. One was the shooting at Branjevo farm which lasted from around 9.00 or 10.00 in the morning until 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then when that ended, there was a request that the accused should participate in another shooting of people who had assembled or had been made to assemble in a public building at Pilica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were two main events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have heard the correction by Mr. Babic concerning the question whether you were not present, but I can tell you this, Mr. Babic, with the consent of Prosecutor counsel, corrected the record by making it clear that the accused did not participate in the second event, he only participated in the first event. You were testifying on 19th November about these matters, and I am reading the transcript, and I observe, tell me if this is correct, that in relation to the first event, you said he, meaning the accused: " ... had understood then what the purpose of the operation was and that he would be involved in the execution of these people." That is in relation to the Branjevo farm shooting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I observe you did not mention his statement that he then acted under duress. Am I right or wrong in so reading the transcript of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are right. At that time I was just explaining the facts as they were reported by Drazen Erdemovic and also the level of corroboration that we had reached at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I shift to the second event which lamentably occurred on that date. I am reading again from the transcript of your evidence. It is in connection with that second event that you then say: "Drazen Erdemovic states that he refused to participate in the second execution and his colleagues did likewise." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on that occasion, you mentioned his statement that he acted under duress, but you mentioned it in connection with his refusal to participate in the second round of shootings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I could say in addition on this, but this is an information that I got from Drazen Erdemovic, the reason why he dared oppose to participate in the second killing was that they already had spent five hours on this killing field, killing all the people who were arriving on the spot, and having fulfilled this part of the assignment, they felt secure enough to oppose the order of the lieutenant colonel, since they had the feeling that they had already done far enough that day, so they had a feeling that this man could not take action against them at that moment, and also the fact that other comrades of him immediately stepped behind him, saying "no, we are not willing to do that". He felt that the lieutenant colonel could not take the risk at that moment to have a kind of rebellion among this execution squad, which was also in -- the confrontation was unuseful, since this officer also had at his disposal a few members of soldiers coming from Bratunac who were obviously volunteered for the task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me give you an opportunity to help the Tribunal by supplementing the transcript a little. We have established, I think, that on 19th November when you were testifying, you did not mention his statement about the duress when speaking of the first set of executions. Was it the case that he might have told you so but you did not remember to tell the Tribunal that on 19th November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the reason why I did not mention any duress at that time was simply because I was not asked about that. I was just requested to explain what had been the -- what was our knowledge of the events, from where we got that knowledge and what was the corroboration that we could provide the court about these events. That was the situation at that time, but at that moment I was not asked what was my feelings, my personal feelings, which are only of my responsibility. Maybe others would have other feelings, but I was not asked about what was my opinion about the duress at that time in November 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I appreciate the answers which you have given me and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WANG
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, I have only one question to you. That is at the very first contact with the accused, Mr. Erdemovic, did he explain to you why he exposed such a serious offence to society and intending to go to The Hague to be tried? Did he explain that to you at this point and did you report that you talked to the Office of the Prosecutor and put it in writing, that is afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He did not explain it in one occasion, in fact the explanation came little bit by little bit through the multiplication of the contacts that we had together. He never made an issue of that at the beginning and we did not also. The first -- the first aim was to get access to the facts that he had the knowledge of and only at a later stage did we deepen the reasons why he made all these efforts to come and testify. The reasons were already quite obvious since the beginning, because he explained how responsible he thought these people were to have put him, who was a soldier, he was doing only sabotage operations and suddenly he was stuck in a huge criminal operation and he was extremely angry about these people who have put him in this situation and explain also the relationship that he had with his commander which was getting worse and worse after some time, and all these explanations came in fact slowly. And the fact is also that if ever they did not have decided to kill him, maybe he would not have made all these efforts to come, so all these situations are a bit melted together, because the fact that he got shot was most probably due to his obvious attitude, not only on the spot when the execution was carried out, but also when he told us bit by bit, he explained to us also what was his behaviour after the massacre when he came back to Bijeljina, he started to drink, did not communicate much more with his wife and had more or less on any occasion arguments with other members of his unit. Some of them were kind of proud of what they had done and instead of staying quiet, he was a bit verbally aggressive to them, so he quickly not only raised suspicion, but he raised the anger of the others against him. This is most probably the reason why at one point they decided to get rid of him. This is the event that triggered the necessity that at this point he had to escape and the best escape he could have at that time was to come and testify to the Tribunal. It was helping his situation and on top of it was providing him with the tools to take a kind of revenge on his commanders and explain exactly what had happened at that time, because he is clearly strongly against this kind of criminal behaviours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WANG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As a result of the questions put to the witness by the judges and the witness's answers, is there anything the Prosecution would like to clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Ruez. You may leave the witness box. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is the only witness the Prosecution was going to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. They are the matters that we wish to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Babic, any evidence you would wish to call in mitigation, whether you wish to call the accused himself or any other witness? We are aware of the witnesses that were called in the previous hearing, Witness X and Witness Y, who were under the Tribunal's protection. We are also aware of the evidence Mr. Erdemovic gave during that hearing, but it is up to you really to decide what to do before this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will not call any witnesses. I suggest that we use the transcript of the testimonies of the witnesses X and Y and they be used in evidence, upon which the determination will be made. Also together with my learned colleague Kostic, I have spoken with the accused Erdemovic, whether he had the strength to testify one more time before this Trial Chamber on his own behalf. He requested, and I am passing on his request to you, if it is not necessary for the Trial Chamber, he would also like to rely on the testimony he gave to the previous Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, we just want to be clear with what you have just said, particularly the last part, that you would rely on the transcripts of evidence which particularly the accused himself gave in the previous Chamber. Is that your decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In which case, besides the transcripts of evidence of Witness X and Y in defence and also the evidence which the accused gave in the previous Trial Chamber, you have no other witnesses to call; that is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: We do not have another witness to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, will you please stand? You have heard what your Defence counsel has said, that in mitigation, the evidence of the witnesses which were called before the previous Trial Chamber gave, that is Witness X and Y for the Defence, and also the evidence that you gave during the hearing before the previous Chamber. The transcripts of that evidence, of the witnesses and yourself, will be used by this Trial Chamber and that you do not wish to give any more evidence yourself in person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you wish to ask any question, I will do so, but honestly speaking, I would prefer not to talk about it any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
