utterances.text: My understanding was that the representative of the Prosecution has also moved that the two reports that we have by the medical commission also be introduced into evidence, and I would just like to make this absolutely clear, and I would like to support that. Also, as stated by my colleague Mr. Kostic, I would like to also move into evidence the statement of the journalist Vasic Janekovic and that would be all the documents we would like to tender into evidence. This would be one issue and as the Defence, we would also like to make some comments before the sentence itself is passed, which regard the sentence itself and the Article 11 of the federal law of the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that you would like to make such submissions. I will return to you later. Can you please sit down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I would just like to be clear in my own mind as to the status of the question and the making of any decision relating to the question whether your client should or should not testify. I understood you to mean that so far as the Defence is concerned, the Defence does not wish Mr. Erdemovic to testify, but that he is available to testify if the Chamber wishes him to testify; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have spoken to Mr. Erdemovic, both myself and my learned colleague Mr. Kostic, on this very topic. It is the eighth time that Mr. Erdemovic is speaking to the matter of his guilt. It is the eighth time that he is reliving the events that he had lived. We have seen some dramatic scenes before this Tribunal, and so we thought that if it is not absolutely necessary we would like whatever he stated on the first through the seventh occasion in evidence. We just wanted to spare him, but he is available for any questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand, and I think I appreciate the humanities which are involved in this aspect of the matter and I would leave it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We shall now hear any submissions that the parties wish to make and will begin with the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I rely on what I said earlier, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Babic or Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Babic and I have split up some of our duties, so I will try to be a bit more brief in regard to my submission. What I wanted to do, because it is my understanding that this may be the first case in front of this Tribunal which first of all is back for a replea, but then in addition to that, that we have an agreement that we have submitted to the court. I want to talk about that just briefly. One I think initial remark is this: the rules and regulations, the Statute of the Tribunal, I have been told by academics is a hybrid of all legal systems. A lawyer from the United States, of course, should not come here and tell you that one system or another is better, but he should tell you that maybe if we take the best of all systems, this system will be much better. Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Niemann and Mr. Babic and I have worked very hard to put together an agreement for your consideration and whereas Mr. Babic, you may want to know, really had no familiarity with such a document, it just is not used in his system, Mr. McCloskey and I, of course, became fast friends, because we are from the same system -- fast friends I mean in the adversarial way, and worked on this agreement because we understood what it meant because we would use it weekly, monthly, daily, for many years of our practice. What is probably more important about that is the fact that we told Mr. Erdemovic that we were working on this, and when he entered the plea in front of you earlier this afternoon, he considered this agreement. I think the agreement has really all of the, I should say, aspects of this case and it also serves the purpose, I think, of everyone involved in this matter: the judges, your Honours, the Prosecution, the Defence and let us not forget one other thing; we also have victims in this case, and I think it serves the needs of the victims. What does it do? There is no need for a long and lengthy trial. Mr. Erdemovic has come in and entered a plea, said he had committed the crimes, and I think that -- he has done that quite speedily. If you know from the record in this case, he entered a plea of guilty at the arraignment. The very first time he appeared in court, he entered the plea. I recall sitting in my living room back in the United States and watching a very dramatic presentation of Mr. Erdemovic pleading guilty. He has been consistent, as you know, seven or eight times. That, of course, I think helps the victims in this case, because they do not have to worry about certain things. That part of the case has been done, has been concluded in a very speedy fashion. I think it unfortunately, obviously the horror of this whole situation is such that I do not want to go much further with it, but I think it does add to some finality in a small piece of this process. The Prosecution was spared a lengthy trial, lots of witnesses, a lot of expenses. You know, when you are sitting in a courtroom like this, with some of the finest minds, with some of the highest ideals, we do not want to talk about finances, because we cannot measure justice in finances, but then I am told when I come here that there are such pressures and it does help the Prosecution, it helps the Tribunal. As far as your Honours are concerned, I think it allows you, if this is done as it was done in this case, it allows you to go on and use your time for other cases, where maybe there are genuine issues. Judicial economy is what we call it in the United States, but I think that is a part of it, and that is important. For the Defence, likewise, we have an agreement. Mr. Babic talks about Rule 11 in the United States. I am not sure if we need to go into that, that is a very specialised rule, where in fact we occasionally get a prior consent on the agreement, including the amount of time to be served. Obviously if the judge does not like it he tells us to go away and do something else, but that is what Rule 11 stands for. Nevertheless for the Defence, we do have some things that are favourable to us, we know what we are pleading guilty to, and then finally, Mr. Erdemovic gets a peace of mind in this situation. He knows what he is going to plead guilty to, he knows what the recommendation is going to be. I think he feels comfortable. You have seen the process this afternoon, his comfort with having entered that plea because he has a man of Mr. Niemann's stature, a seasoned Prosecutor in his country, here in the Tribunal, he knows what a case is worth. He has fought the wars here for three years, he knows that his recommendations are good, they are sound, and, of course, we all hope that you would follow the Prosecutor's recommendation. That is our hope, that is our recommendation. Also by the way, pursuant to the agreement, we also feel that the seven year sentence is an appropriate one. So those are my remarks about this plea agreement. I think it is a good instrument, it is a good document, I hope that the Tribunal, the other Chambers would use it if there are appropriate circumstances. In this particular case, I think it is a very fair resolution of this particular case and it is fair to everyone who is concerned in this case, so again I apologise for maybe trying to be a little preachy about what this stands for, but I hope that you understand my position, that I do want to see Mr. Erdemovic receive a sentence that is consistent with the plea agreement. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on this occasion, I would like to express my special satisfaction that in a procedure that has raised many legal and moral issues, we as a Defence and the learned colleagues of the Prosecution have reached very similar or I should say literally similar positions and legal arguments. I think that until now, the proceedings have confirmed this, before this Trial Chamber. In this phase of the proceedings, before the passing of the sentence, I would just like to make several comments which the Trial Chamber I hope may find useful when determining whether to accept the agreement and what punishment it should pass. Today, the accused Erdemovic pleaded, and I have counted these pleas, because I was present at all of them, it is the eighth time, and this time he pleaded guilty for the war crime. In this situation, that is just before the punishment has been determined, the Defence would like to point out that the issue before us is not just a legal one, it is equally, if not more, a moral issue. So someone's plea of guilty and admission of his guilt and the severity of punishment is not only a legal issue but also a moral issue. This is the case not only in the case of particular country but also for the international community which is a community of all the nations. It also affects the victims of the crimes, as well as the perpetrator. The Defence believes that this complex approach is the only one that is possible and I am grateful that the Prosecution adopted this position and I am hopeful that the Trial Chamber would do so as well. I would like to remind the Trial Chamber of the voluntary, informed and unequivocal statements of the accused Erdemovic about his guilt. These statements should, above all, be taken as his moral attitude towards the truth on the one hand and as a plea for understanding of how far the limits of the abuse of man in this region were stretched, not only in his local environment but also in the wider scope. Also, his moral attitude towards the truth must be proportionately reflected in the punishment. It must be satisfactory to the victims, acceptable and beneficial to the national and international communities and fair towards the accused himself. With all due respect, I think that this should be the approach that the Trial Chamber should adopt when determining the proper sentence. I will now move on to the mitigating circumstances, taking into account what the learned colleagues from the Prosecution have already argued. The proceedings so far confirm beyond any doubt that there is a number of mitigating circumstances in favour of Mr. Erdemovic, and I will try to enumerate them. First, the accused Erdemovic found himself caught up in the vortex of war which was caused by the conflict of three ethnic communities, without his own will. This conflict assumed the aspect of a total war, including an element which played a greater role than at any time in the modern history, which was this element of the ethnic cleansing. The criminal act in which the accused Erdemovic took part as a direct perpetrator without a doubt falls within the scope of the most serious violations of international law, but the accused Erdemovic is not creator here, or an ideologue, or somebody who issued orders. He is not a religious or a nationalist fanatic. Nor is he a sadistic soldier, but rather a victim which begets further victims; a simple instrument for killing, which had to kill lest it be killed. That the accused Erdemovic could in no way have avoided the situation in which he unforeseeably and suddenly found himself, that before the commission of the crime, he at the scene made a hopeful but futile attempt to resist the implacable order of the superior; that the accused Erdemovic proceeded to commit the crime under irresistible duress as was pointed out by the learned colleagues from the Prosecution; that he pleaded guilty for the crime of -- war crime rather than crime against humanity, and his plea for the first time has spelled out clearly that the crime against humanity is a more serious crime of the two. Further, that Mr. Erdemovic found himself in a position of clear and present danger to his own life and that of his family's, and he was in a position where he either had to shoot or he would be shot; that all this caused Erdemovic fear for his own life and that of his family, to which he found no alternative, no alternative in his local environment and anywhere in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and that therefore his intent in committing the crime was significantly diminished, and here I would also like to respectfully refer to the findings of the medical commission. That during the commission of this crime, he tried to save the life of one person, but he failed to do so, and then that he refused, and this time it was with the support of the members of this unit, this was in Pilica, he refused to take part in the execution at the social hall in Pilica. He found inner strength and this was also supported by the comments of the learned colleagues of the Prosecution, who explained why he did so; that in the end, Erdemovic himself became a victim of his own "fellow soldier", who gravely wounded him, so that he managed to turn himself in and appear before this Tribunal, thanks only to the successful efforts of physicians in the former Yugoslavia and here in The Hague and the Registry of this Tribunal; that the accused Erdemovic held a low rank in the military units in which he was. As he said, he at first held the lowest rank up from the private, and only for one month. That the testimony of the Witness X confirms without a doubt that the accused Erdemovic never before committed any crimes against any members of the army; in fact on the contrary, he let a man go and he saved his life. He did everything he could in order to let the public know the facts of this committed crime and he was determined to appear to answer to them before this very Tribunal. In all his statements, from the first one he gave to all the ones he gave to this Tribunal, he admitted his participation in the commission of this crime and virtually accused himself or brought himself before this Tribunal, whereby he expressed his moral stance and a strong sense of remorse. That from the start of these proceedings, he has significantly co-operated with the Prosecution, as was also supported by the Prosecution today, and that he also testified as part of this co-operation, he testified in the hearings according to the Rule 61. That throughout his stay in the detention, he behaved in accordance with the rules of this institution and very correctly, and based on the information that I regularly received from the officials in the detention unit, he clearly expressed strong remorse for having taken part in the commission of the crime, as was also corroborated by the witness Jean-Rene Ruez. We would also like the Trial Chamber to take into account several other issues. It is the personal circumstances of the accused Erdemovic, that is his personality, his character, his family and social background. At the time of the commission of the crime, the accused Erdemovic was only 23 years old. He is a Croat and a Catholic. He comes from a working class family, in which the children were brought up in the spirit of religious and ethnic tolerance, and as Yugoslavs. This he adopted in his own life without reservation, and he acted accordingly. The different religions and ethnic groups in his environment were his true wealth, and as crowning proof of this all, he married a woman from another ethnic and religious group, with whom he has a three year old child. His family lives in the Tuzla area, which is where they lived before the war and during the war, and they have fallen on hard times. Therefore his family will suffer hardship due to his serving a prison sentence. He did everything he could to avoid these winds of war and to leave the country and go abroad with his family. However, unfortunately, he did not succeed. So the confluence of many circumstances in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and I think that the Trial Chamber is aware of this, and the unavailability of other choice took him to all three warring sides. This was his modus vivendi and not only his, this was a fate shared by all. He never belonged to any nationalist party. He resisted as much as he could all propaganda advocating intolerance, just as he was taught at school, by the community and family. He has no criminal record, and he does not even have any misdemeanour charges against him. All this makes it clear that the accused Erdemovic poses no danger for his environment and that his character is reformable. This is also borne out by the expert commission findings. The Defence submits to the Trial Chamber that these mitigating circumstances should be taken as real and founded. They should be taken also as a basis on which the accused, Erdemovic, has reached a plea agreement with the Prosecution, having admitted his guilt, taking into consideration that a seven year sentence is adequate, bearing in mind all the circumstances, and this is what he has to give back to his victims. I want to give you my personal view on this. I believe that this is going to be a recurrent nightmare for the accused, Erdemovic, for the rest of his life. Therefore, the Defence believes that the agreement which has been reached between Erdemovic and the Prosecution, all elements of punishment will be satisfied, both the national and international ones. In closing, I would like to add that this Trial Chamber, based on Rule 101(B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, that the Trial Chamber will take into account the time that the accused Erdemovic has spent in detention, which is close to two years. I would just like to add one more thing, that this Trial Chamber will also consider its decision in which host country the accused, Erdemovic, is going to go to serve out his sentence. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: May I add something, just very minor. I believe that we have agreed with Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Niemann that Mr. Erdemovic was arrested on March 3rd 1996, which would give us approximately 22 months and 11 days in custody. If I am off, I certainly would stand to be corrected. I think I am fairly close, to give you an idea as to his time in custody before his sentencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am sure we can reach exactly what that date is. I know we have the documents, but it may need closer looking into to double-check the exact date. It should not be a problem. It should be very close if not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: We may be able to make a stipulation to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: On this issue of taking into account previous incarceration, I would like to be clear with the parties. It is the time in detention after the Tribunal came on the scene that matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honours. That is the view of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The understanding between the parties is that that previous detention time is to be deducted from whatever sentence of imprisonment, if such a sentence is imposed, were to be ordered; that is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: That was the agreement we reached, your Honour. That was our agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. So if your Honours were to impose a particular sentence of a number of years, it would be that sentence commenced at the time he started his custody in The Hague, so it would date from that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we have come to the end of our proceedings. Unless there are any other matters that the parties would like to mention at this stage? Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I just wish to confirm your Honours. I have been handed a document that suggests that Mr. Erdemovic was transferred to the Tribunal on 30th March 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: 30th March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Not 3rd March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He was arrested earlier on 2nd March and transferred on 30th March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would not the Defence be suggesting that from the time of his arrest his status would be one of incarceration on behalf of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not sure whether that is what is being suggested by the Defence, but the position that we have taken is that it should be from the moment of incarceration in The Hague, which is 30th March. We do that based on the decision of the Chamber in the Tadic case, which also commenced its period of consideration as the period from incarceration in The Hague. Fortunately for Mr. Erdemovic in this case it is a matter of some 20 days, but nevertheless I would not belittle that in any sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: If I may add, your Honours, I personally would not agree to this, but in the interests of expediency, we wish to support the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This brings our proceedings today to a close. The sentencing judgement of this Trial Chamber will be delivered in due course in open court. The parties will be given advance warning of the date of delivery of judgement, which will be in public. This session is now adjourned. (5.30 pm)
